Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette:
Elsa has been at sea for fifty-four of her seventy-six years, and the bridge of her cargo ship, the *North Star*, has always been her sanctuary. Now, it feels more like a cage. The six months since the incident have corroded the quiet confidence she once took for granted. She finds herself staying on the bridge long after her watch is over, poring over nautical charts for routes she has known by heart for decades. She throws herself into the work, finding any task to occupy her hands and, more importantly, her mind. Polishing the brass on the binnacle until it gleams, reorganizing the logbooks, running diagnostics twice over—anything to keep the silence at bay. In the silence, the images come.

They aren't hazy or dreamlike; they are a series of stark, still photographs that flash behind her eyes with brutal clarity. The protest had been peaceful, a gathering of older activists concerned about port pollution. She had been standing near the back, holding a sign. The first image is the line of police in riot gear, shields catching the afternoon sun. The second is the face of a young officer, his expression a blank mask as he shoved an elderly man beside her. The third, the one that always steals her breath, is the cracked pavement rushing up to meet her cheek. When these memories surface, it is not like watching a film of something that happened long ago. She is there again. She can feel the grit of the asphalt against her skin, hear the flat, percussive sound of a baton hitting a shield, and feel the helpless shock of the impact that sent her sprawling. Her heart begins to hammer against her ribs just as it did then, a frantic bird trapped in her chest.

In the long, empty nights at sea, she lies in her bunk and lets the questions circle endlessly. Why her? She had done nothing, said nothing. She had simply been there. Why had that one officer chosen to shove her, a woman in her seventies, to the ground? She goes over and over the moment, trying to find a reason, a logic that simply isn't there. The lack of an answer is its own kind of torment. This constant questioning has become a second, unwelcome crew member on her voyages. Alongside it is a profound sense of loss for the woman she used to be. Before the event, she was Captain Elsa Brandt, unflappable, respected, a woman who had faced down North Atlantic gales without a tremor. Now, she feels brittle and afraid. She dwells on that former self, the one who could calmly give orders during a squall, and wonders if that person is gone for good.

The change has not gone unnoticed. Last month, while docking in Baltimore, a Port Authority officer came aboard for a routine inspection. The moment he stepped onto the bridge, in his crisp uniform and polished boots, Elsa froze. The image of the officer at the protest—the same impassive face, the same rigid posture—slammed into her mind. For a terrifying second, she wasn't on the bridge of the *North Star*; she was on the pavement, gasping for air. Her first mate had to step in and answer the officer’s questions, covering for her sudden, inexplicable silence. The shame of that moment was a physical weight. Her crew’s worried glances now feel like accusations. She, their captain, had faltered. It was after that incident, realizing her command and the safety of her crew were at risk, that Elsa finally made the call. She is seeking help not just to quiet the images, but to find her way back to the woman who was master of her ship, and of herself.
